title: Safeguarding adults and children
blurb: Recognise the types of abuse, apply the Care Act s42 criteria and six principles, and share information to protect children.
question: Mrs Wood, 82, lives alone and receives daily care visits. She tells the community nurse her carer has been keeping her bank card "to help" and she often has no money for food. What type of abuse is this, and what should the nurse do?

teach.h: Safeguarding: protecting people's right to live safely
teach.body: Safeguarding means protecting a person's right to live in safety, free from abuse and neglect. Proficiency P3.9 asks you to recognise and assess people at risk of harm and act promptly to safeguard. For adults in England the legal framework is the Care Act 2014; for children it is the Children Acts and Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026. Code 17: raise concerns immediately and share information if someone may be at risk of harm.
teach.cite: Care Act 2014 s42; Care and support statutory guidance ch 14; Code 17.1-17.3

teach.caption: Local authorities should not limit their view of what constitutes abuse or neglect.

letters.word: Empowerment: supported to make own decisions
Protection: support for those in greatest need

teach.caption: Care and support statutory guidance para 14.13.

teach.body: Safeguarding is person-led and outcome-focused. An enquiry usually starts by asking the adult their views and wishes, which often determine what happens next (para 14.93). If an adult with capacity does not want action, that does not stop you sharing information with relevant professionals to assess risk and check they are not being coerced; tell them unless doing so would increase the risk (14.92). Action may still be needed if others are at risk or a crime has occurred (14.95).
teach.cite: Care and support statutory guidance paras 14.92-14.95

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Wood and her bank card
teach.body: Mrs Wood has care needs, is experiencing financial abuse (misuse of her money and possessions) and, because of her needs, cannot easily protect herself: the s42 criteria are met. The nurse listens, reassures her she was right to speak, asks what she would like to happen, and explains she must share the concern. She raises a safeguarding concern with the local authority the same day, informs her own safeguarding lead and records Mrs Wood's words accurately.

rows.label: Consent to share
values: Seek it; may share to assess risk

teach.caption: Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 replaced the 2023 edition (March 2026).

teach.body: From 30 September 2026, Children Act 2004 s16LA requires bodies under the s11 duty, including NHS bodies, to share information they consider relevant to safeguarding or promoting a child's welfare with other such bodies where it may help their safeguarding functions. There is no threshold, consent is not required, and the disclosure does not breach confidence, unless sharing would be more harmful to the child than not sharing. When an adult patient has children, consider the children's safety too.

teach.text: Don't wait for proof. You raise a concern on reasonable suspicion; the enquiry establishes facts. And don't investigate yourself: listen, reassure, don't promise secrecy, don't ask leading questions, record the person's own words, and refer. Also, an adult's refusal of action does not stop you sharing with professionals to assess risk.

items: s42: care and support needs + abuse or neglect (or risk) + unable to protect themselves because of those needs.
Ten types of abuse in para 14.17, including organisational, discriminatory, modern slavery and self-neglect.
Six principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, accountability.
Making Safeguarding Personal: ask the adult what outcomes they want.
Children: Working Together 2026; s16LA duty to share, no threshold, no consent needed.

summary: You can now identify the types of abuse, apply the s42 criteria and the six principles, involve adults in their own safeguarding, and share information about children under the s16LA duty and Working Together 2026.

A.q: Mrs Wood, 82, receives daily care visits. She tells the community nurse her carer keeps her bank card and she often has no money for food. Which type of abuse is this?
options: Organisational abuse
Psychological or emotional abuse
Neglect and acts of omission
Financial or material abuse
A.why: Care and support statutory guidance para 14.17: financial or material abuse includes theft and the misuse or misappropriation of property, possessions or benefits.

whyNot.0: Organisational abuse arises from an institution's routines and practices.
whyNot.1: Psychological abuse involves threats, humiliation or control; the core issue here is her money.
whyNot.2: The lack of food results from her money being taken, so financial abuse is the best fit.

A.q: A nurse joining a residential home finds all residents are got up and dressed by 6 am to suit staff rotas and toileted at fixed times. Which type of abuse does this suggest?
options: Organisational abuse
Discriminatory abuse
Self-neglect by residents
Physical abuse by staff
A.why: Organisational abuse includes neglect and poor practice resulting from an organisation's structure, policies, processes and practices (para 14.17).

whyNot.1: Discriminatory abuse targets people because of a protected characteristic.
whyNot.2: Self-neglect concerns a person not caring for themselves.
whyNot.3: Nothing describes force or physical harm.

A.q: Mr Gray, 70, has capacity and a physical disability. He says his son pushes him when angry but asks for minimal involvement. The team chooses the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk. Which principle is this?
options: The prevention principle
The protection principle
The proportionality principle
The partnership principle
A.why: Proportionality: the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk presented (para 14.13).

whyNot.0: Prevention is about acting before harm occurs.
whyNot.1: Protection is support and representation for those in greatest need.
whyNot.3: Partnership is local solutions through services working with communities.

B.q: A ward nurse is completing an adult safeguarding referral in England. For the s42 duty, the adult must have care and support needs and be experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect. What is the third criterion?
options: They are aged 65 or over at the time of the concern
They lack mental capacity to make decisions about their safety
They receive services funded by the local authority
As a result of those needs, they cannot protect themselves
B.why: Care Act 2014 s42(1)(c): as a result of those needs, the adult is unable to protect themselves from the abuse or neglect or the risk of it.

whyNot.0: There is no age criterion in s42.
whyNot.1: Lacking capacity is not a criterion; adults with capacity can meet s42.
whyNot.2: The duty applies whether or not the local authority is meeting the needs.

B.q: Mrs Ahmed, 66, has capacity and care needs after a stroke. She says her husband sometimes slaps her but does not want anything done. What should the nurse do?
options: Respect her wishes and record the disclosure fully in her notes
Share it with relevant professionals through the safeguarding lead
Tell her husband that the staff are aware and will be watching him
Wait until she discloses again before taking any action
B.why: Statutory guidance para 14.92: an adult with capacity not wanting action does not preclude sharing with relevant professionals to assess risk and check she is not coerced. It is good practice to tell her unless that increases risk.

whyNot.0: Recording alone does not allow the risk to be assessed.
whyNot.2: Confronting the alleged abuser could increase the risk to her.
whyNot.3: Delay leaves a disclosed risk unassessed.

B.q: Mr Lee, 58, has care needs and has been financially exploited by a neighbour. At the start of the safeguarding enquiry, what does Making Safeguarding Personal require first?
options: Ask Mr Lee what outcomes he wants from the enquiry
Report the neighbour to the police for investigation
Arrange a best interests meeting with his family
Move Mr Lee's money into an account the council controls
B.why: Making Safeguarding Personal is person-led and outcome-focused; an enquiry usually starts with asking the adult their views and wishes (para 14.93).

whyNot.1: Police involvement may follow, but the adult's views come first in a person-led approach.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests he lacks capacity, so best interests does not apply.
whyNot.3: This is a disproportionate step taken without his views.

C.q: In an emergency department in England, Kerry, 29, is treated for intoxication. She mentions her 3-year-old son is at home alone, and asks staff not to tell anyone. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask her consent again when she has sobered up
Respect her wishes, as she is an adult with capacity
Record it and inform her GP in the discharge summary letter
Share the information with children's social care now
C.why: Children Act 2004 s16LA (in force 30 September 2026) requires NHS bodies to share information relevant to safeguarding a child, with no threshold and without consent; it does not breach confidence. The child needs urgent protection.

whyNot.0: Consent is not required, and waiting leaves a young child unsafe.
whyNot.1: Her autonomy does not override the duty to safeguard her son.
whyNot.2: A discharge summary is far too slow for a child alone now.

C.q: Miss Patel, 45, has a learning disability and substantial difficulty understanding the safeguarding process. Her only relative is the person suspected of abusing her. What should happen?
options: Her relative supports her through the whole enquiry
The local authority arranges an independent advocate
The ward nurse acts as her advocate in all the meetings
The enquiry continues without her involvement
C.why: Care Act 2014 s68 and statutory guidance para 7.3: an independent advocate must be arranged where the adult has substantial difficulty being involved and there is no appropriate person to support them.

whyNot.0: The suspected abuser is not an appropriate person to support her.
whyNot.2: The ward nurse is not independent of the process.
whyNot.3: Making Safeguarding Personal requires her involvement, with support.

C.q: During a home visit, a district nurse finds Mr Price, 79, who lives alone, in a cluttered, unheated house, with untreated leg wounds and no food. He has capacity and refuses help. Which type of concern is this?
options: Organisational abuse
Neglect by a carer
Self-neglect
Discriminatory abuse
C.why: Self-neglect covers neglecting personal hygiene, health or surroundings, including hoarding (para 14.17). It may not prompt a s42 enquiry; a response depends on his ability to protect himself, assessed case by case.

whyNot.0: No institution or service is involved.
whyNot.1: He lives alone and no carer has withheld care.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests he is targeted because of a protected characteristic.

reteach.title: Recognise, respond, refer, record
reteach.question: If someone discloses abuse to you, what are the four things you do?

blocks.h: Your role is to raise, not to investigate
blocks.body: RECOGNISE the signs, including the less obvious types: organisational, discriminatory, modern slavery, self-neglect. RESPOND: listen calmly, reassure, don't promise secrecy, ask what they want. REFER: to your safeguarding lead and the local authority (adults) or children's social care (children), sharing information as the law allows. RECORD: the person's own words, dates, times and what you did.

blocks.text: Never promise to keep a disclosure secret. Explain who you will tell and why.

explain.body: The local authority must make enquiries where an adult has needs for care and support, is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and as a result of those needs cannot protect themselves (Care Act 2014 s42).

test.q: Which adult most clearly meets all three s42 criteria?
options: A fit 40-year-old man robbed in the street at night
A woman with dementia whose son takes her pension
A man who chooses to drink heavily at home
A nurse bullied by her ward manager at work
test.why: She has care and support needs, is experiencing financial abuse, and because of her dementia may be unable to protect herself.

whyNot.0: A crime victim without care and support needs does not meet s42.
whyNot.2: There is no abuse by another person and no indication he cannot protect himself.
whyNot.3: Workplace bullying of a staff member is an employment matter, not s42.

explain.body: Physical, domestic violence, sexual, psychological, financial or material, modern slavery, discriminatory, organisational, neglect and acts of omission, self-neglect (para 14.17). Look for patterns, not just single incidents.

test.q: A care worker repeatedly mocks a resident's accent and religion. Which type of abuse is this?
options: Psychological abuse
Organisational abuse
Discriminatory abuse
Physical abuse
test.why: Discriminatory abuse includes harassment or slurs because of race, religion or other characteristics (para 14.17).

whyNot.0: It is psychologically harmful, but the defining feature is targeting race and religion.
whyNot.1: It is one worker's behaviour, not an institutional practice.

explain.body: Empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, accountability. Making Safeguarding Personal: ask the adult what outcomes they want; share with professionals to assess risk even if they refuse action.

test.q: A nurse asks a woman disclosing abuse what she would like to happen next. Which principle does this best reflect?
options: Accountability
Prevention
Empowerment
Protection
test.why: Empowerment: people being supported and encouraged to make their own decisions; 'I am asked what I want as the outcomes' (para 14.13).

whyNot.0: Accountability is about transparency in safeguarding roles.
whyNot.1: Prevention is acting before harm occurs.
whyNot.3: Protection is support for those in greatest need.

explain.body: Working Together 2026 is the current statutory guidance in England. Under s16LA (from 30 September 2026), NHS bodies must share information relevant to a child's safety with other safeguarding bodies: no threshold, no consent needed, no breach of confidence.

items.label: s16LA duty to share in force

test.q: Under s16LA, when may an NHS nurse decide not to share information relevant to a child's safety with children's services?
options: When the parent refuses consent
When it would be more harmful to the child
When the concern is below the referral threshold
When the information was given in confidence
test.why: s16LA: the duty applies unless disclosure would be more detrimental to the child than not disclosing. There is no threshold and consent is not required.

whyNot.0: Consent is not required under s16LA.
whyNot.3: Disclosure under s16LA does not breach any obligation of confidence.
